Physics Lab 4

Water Splash

Drop a ball of water into a pool, bake the splash with Mantaflow, and render it as real water in Blender.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how Blender simulates water: the three jobs an object can have (Domain, Flow, Effector), what Resolution Divisions really means, why a fluid has to be baked, and how to make the result look like water instead of grey jelly.

You need Blender 4.2 or newer and a mouse with a scroll wheel (laptop trackpad? see this fix). This lab takes about two lessons, with a bake that runs by itself for a few minutes. Save your file as PhysicsLab4_WaterSplash_YourName.blend before anything else.

You’ve got it when you can

  • say what the Domain, a Flow and an Effector each do
  • build a set with exact numbers and check it is inside the domain
  • explain Resolution Divisions as a cell size and a bake time
  • set the cache to All, bake, and free the bake to change a number
  • make a water material that EEVEE can see through
  • light the scene, place the camera, render a still and a movie

The plan

Five parts. Each one ends with a rendered picture of what your scene should look like.

  1. Part 1The one-click versionSteps 1–2
  2. Part 2Build the setSteps 3–7
  3. Part 3Three jobs, then bakeSteps 8–12
  4. Part 4Make it look like waterSteps 13–15
  5. Part 5RenderStep 16

A box full of cells

Blender does not simulate water as a surface. It chops the domain box into a grid of small cells, fills the wet ones with thousands of tiny particles, and every frame works out where the particles go: gravity pulls them down, pressure stops them squashing into each other, walls and effectors push them back. Then it wraps a smooth skin (the mesh) around wherever the particles are. That skin is the water you see, and it is the only part you give a material to.

So everything in this lab is about the box and its cells. Resolution Divisions is how many cells across the box; the cell size is the smallest detail the splash can have, and the bake time grows brutally as the cells shrink. A Flow object just says which cells start full. An Effector says which cells are solid. The Domain is the box itself, and nothing exists outside it.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Domain
The object (a cube) that defines the box the simulation runs in. Water cannot leave it. It is also the object that becomes the water mesh.
Flow
An object that makes water: Geometry (becomes water once), Inflow (pours), Outflow (drains).
Effector
A solid object the water flows around. Collision type; Is Planar for thin sheets.
Resolution Divisions
How many cells across the domain’s longest side. 64 on a 4 m box = 6.25 cm cells.
FLIP / particles
The method: particles carry the water between cells; the grid solves pressure. 8 to 16 particles per wet cell.
Mesh (panel)
The skin built around the particles each frame, at Upres Factor 2 (twice the resolution) so it looks smoother than the physics.
Cache: Replay / Modular / All
Replay simulates as you play and saves nothing; Modular bakes data and mesh separately; All bakes everything with one button.
Bake All / Free All
Compute and save every frame to the cache folder beside your .blend; delete it again so numbers can change.
Border Collisions
Six checkboxes: which domain walls are solid. All on by default (an aquarium).
IOR
Index of refraction: how much a material bends light. Water 1.33, glass 1.45, diamond 2.4.
Transmission
How much light passes through a surface instead of bouncing off. 1 for water and glass.
Raytraced Transmission / Raytracing
The material switch and the render switch that let EEVEE trace light through transparent things.
X-ray (Alt+Z)
See-through viewport, so you can see inside the domain cube.

Part 1

The one-click version

Tools: the File menu, Object › Quick Effects › Quick Liquid, Space, File › Revert.

Blender can turn the default cube into water with one menu item. It is a bad splash, but it shows the three jobs (Domain, Flow, Effector) in sixty seconds, so you know what you are building when you do it properly in Parts 2 and 3.

How the steps work

Each step has a Where line (which part of the Blender window to look at), a Watch animation of the mouse doing the step (pause it, drag the slider, or use the arrow buttons to go one move at a time), and a Do this list of the same moves as a, b, c. Do one move, look at the animation, do the next. The drawings are simplified, not screenshots: the words and positions match Blender, the exact colours and spacing may not. The water in the drawings is a cartoon; the water in the checkpoint photos is the real thing.

  1. Start fresh and save

    Layout workspace › the File menu at the very top-left.

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › New › General. You get a cube, a camera and a light. Keep the cube this time.
    2. b
      File › Save As. In your Physics labs folder, type PhysicsLab4_WaterSplash_YourName and click Save Blender File.

    You should now see: the window title shows your file name.

    Why save before anything else?

    A fluid bake is not stored inside the .blend; it is a folder of files (cache_fluid_…) that Blender writes next to the .blend. In an unsaved file that folder goes to a temporary place and vanishes when you close Blender. Save first, and keep the .blend and its cache folder together.

  2. Quick Liquid, then undo it

    The viewport header’s Object menu, the Outliner, the Timeline, the File menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the cube. Viewport header › Object › Quick Effects › Quick Liquid.
    2. b
      Look: the viewport switched to Wireframe, a tall box called Liquid Domain wraps the cube, and the Outliner lists both. Click the Domain, then the cube, and look at the Physics tab of each.
    3. c
      Hover the viewport, Space. The cube turns into a cloud of dots that slumps to the floor of the box. Slow, because it is simulating as it plays. Space to stop.
    4. d
      File › Revert, click Revert. Your saved file is back, with the plain cube.

    You should now see: particles falling inside a wireframe box, then, after Revert, the ordinary grey cube again.

    What did Quick Liquid actually do?

    Three things you will do by hand in Part 3: it made the cube a Flow (Liquid, Geometry), added a cube around it as the Domain (Liquid), and gave the Domain a glass material. It skipped the Effector, used the lowest resolution (32) and a Replay cache that saves nothing. Good for a look, useless for a render.

End of Part 1. Nothing to save: Revert already put the file back.

Part 2

Build the set

Tools: Add › Mesh, the sidebar (N), F2, the Material tab, Alt+Z.

Five objects, every one with exact numbers: a floor, a slab that will become the pool, a block for the water to hit, a ball that will become the drop, and the box that everything happens in. Nothing has physics yet.

  1. The floor

    The Add menu, the sidebar, the Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the cube, X, Delete. Add › Mesh › Plane. S, 8, Enter: a 16 m floor.
    2. b
      Sidebar (N if it is hidden): Location Z -0.05.
    3. c
      F2, type Floor, Enter. Material tab › New › Base Color Hex C9C2B2, Roughness 0.6.

    You should now see: a big sand-coloured floor, 5 cm below the grid.

    Why -0.05?

    The domain box and the pool slab will both have a face at height 0. Two faces in exactly the same place flicker in the viewport (z-fighting). Dropping the floor 5 cm keeps it out of the way; the water itself never gets below 0.

  2. The pool slab

    The Add menu, the sidebar.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cube. Sidebar: Scale X 2.2, Y 2.2, Z 0.3. Location stays 0, 0, 0.
    2. b
      F2, type Pool, Enter.

    You should now see: a flat grey slab 4.4 m wide and 60 cm thick, half of it under the floor. Its top is at 0.3 m: the water line.

    Why wider than the box?

    The domain box will be 4 m wide; the slab is 4.4 m. Water can only exist inside the domain, so the extra 20 cm on each side is simply ignored. Making the slab bigger than the box guarantees the pool reaches every wall with no gap, and no face sits exactly on a wall.

  3. The block

    The Add menu, the sidebar, the Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cube. Sidebar: Location X 1, Z 0.35. Scale X 0.4, Y 0.4, Z 0.4.
    2. b
      F2, type Block, Enter. Material tab › New › Base Color Hex 6E6A66, Roughness 0.7.

    You should now see: an 80 cm stone block standing on the floor to the right of centre, its top 45 cm above the slab.

    Why 0.35?

    The block is 0.8 m tall, so its middle is 0.4 m above its base. The floor is at -0.05, so Location Z 0.35 stands it on the floor, poking through the slab.

  4. The drop

    Add › Mesh › UV Sphere, the sidebar, the right-click menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. Sidebar: Location Z 2.6. Scale X 0.5, Y 0.5, Z 0.5.
    2. b
      Right-click › Shade Smooth (looks only). F2, type Drop, Enter. No material: it will be hidden later.

    You should now see: a 1 m ball hanging in the air, its bottom 1.8 m above the water line.

    How long will it fall?

    From rest, 1.8 m takes 0.6 s: at 24 frames a second, the drop hits the pool around frame 15. Blender’s gravity is the real 9.81 m/s², so a bigger drop height means a longer wait and a bigger splash.

  5. The box

    Add › Mesh › Cube, the sidebar, Alt+Z.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cube. Sidebar: Location Z 2. Scale X 2, Y 2, Z 2. F2, type Domain, Enter.
    2. b
      It hides everything. Hover the viewport, Alt+Z: X-ray. Now you see through it.
    3. c
      Check: the slab pokes out of the box sides (fine), the block and the drop are completely inside (required).

    You should now see: a see-through 4 m cube sitting on the floor with the block, the drop and most of the slab inside it.

    Why not just scale it to fit?

    Water only exists inside the domain, so its size decides the whole simulation: a bigger box with the same Resolution Divisions means bigger cells and a lumpier splash. 4 m is big enough that the crown does not hit the ceiling and small enough for 6 cm cells at 64 divisions.

End of Part 2. Save.

Part 3

Three jobs, then bake

Tools: the Physics tab: Fluid as Domain, Flow and Effector; the Cache panel; Bake All.

The Physics tab has one button, Fluid, and one dropdown that gives an object its job. Domain for the box, Flow for the slab and the drop, Effector for the block. Then tell the cache to save everything, bake, and watch.

Three jobs

A flat toy version of the scene. Untick a job and play to see what goes missing.

  1. The box is the Domain

    The Physics tab (blue orbit icon) with the Domain selected.

    Predict first: The box is 4 m wide. With 64 divisions, how big is one cell? With 32? With 128?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Domain (its orange outline). Physics tab › Fluid. Type: Domain.
    2. b
      Domain Type: Liquid (it starts as Gas, for smoke).
    3. c
      Resolution Divisions 64.

    You should now see: a long Fluid panel, and a tiny white cube at one corner of the box: one cell, 6.25 cm.

    What is a division?

    The domain is chopped into cells, 64 across its longest side, so 64 × 64 × 64 = 262 144 cells of 6.25 cm. The water is tracked by particles moving between cells, and the splash can have no detail smaller than a cell. Double the number and the bake takes about 16 times longer, not 2.

  2. The slab and the drop are Flow

    The Physics tab, twice.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Pool (or its name in the Outliner). Physics tab › Fluid › Type: Flow. Flow Type: Liquid (it starts as Smoke).
    2. b
      Click the Drop. Physics tab › Fluid › Type: Flow. Flow Type: Liquid.
    3. c
      Flow Behavior stays Geometry for both. Nothing changes in the viewport yet.

    You should now see: both objects show a Flow panel with Flow Type Liquid and Flow Behavior Geometry.

    Geometry, Inflow, Outflow?

    Geometry: the object’s shape becomes water once, at frame 1, and the object is then ignored. Inflow: the shape keeps pouring new water every frame, like a tap (that is what the old sheet used, so the box slowly filled up instead of splashing). Outflow: the shape swallows water, like a drain.

  3. The block is an Effector

    The Physics tab with the Block selected.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Block. Physics tab › Fluid › Type: Effector.
    2. b
      Read, change nothing: Effector Type Collision, Surface Thickness 0, Use Effector ticked, Is Planar unticked.

    You should now see: a short Effector panel. The block now counts as solid.

    Does the floor need anything?

    No. The domain’s six walls are solid by default (Fluid panel › Border Collisions, all ticked), and the bottom wall is at height 0, so the water stands on it. The Floor object is scenery for the render; the water never sees it. The same goes for anything without Fluid physics: it is invisible to the water.

  4. Cache to All, then Bake All

    The Timeline’s End box, the Physics tab scrolled down to Cache.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: End 100. Click the Domain. Physics tab, scroll to Cache: End 100.
    2. b
      Type: All (it starts as Replay). A Bake All button appears. Click it.
    3. c
      A bar at the bottom counts to 100: two to five minutes at 64. Esc pauses it. When the button says Free All, hover the viewport and press Space.

    You should now see: frame 15: the drop hits. Frame 22: a crater with a rim. Frame 30: the wave climbs the box walls. Frame 100: nearly calm. Scrubbing is instant.

    Why All, and why bake at all?

    Replay simulates while you play and keeps nothing, so every play is slow and the render would have no water at all. All saves the particles and the water surface mesh for every frame in the cache folder next to your .blend. Free All deletes them if you want to change a number.

  1. Tidy up

    Alt+Z, the Outliner’s eye icons, the orange Object tab › Visibility, the right-click menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport, Alt+Z: X-ray off. The water is a solid grey mesh now.
    2. b
      Outliner: click the eye next to Drop and next to Pool. For each one: Object tab (orange square) › Visibility › untick Renders.
    3. c
      Click the water. Right-click › Shade Smooth.

    You should now see: only the water and the block, the water smooth-shaded. Playing still works: the sources were only needed at frame 1 and are baked in.

    Why two hides?

    The eye hides an object in the viewport only; a hidden object still renders. Visibility › Renders is the one the camera obeys. Hiding after the bake is safe: the cache already has everything it needs.

End of Part 3. Save.

Part 4

Make it look like water

Tools: the Material tab, the Material Settings panel, the Render tab, the Shading workspace, the World and Light tabs, the camera.

Grey lumps become water with a material that lets light through and bends it. Then tiles under the water so you can see the bending, the same sky and sun as Labs 2 and 3, and a camera with exact numbers.

  1. A water material

    The Material tab with the Domain selected, its Settings panel, then the Render tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the water. Material tab › New. Name it Water. Base Color › Hex B0D4E8. Roughness 0.02. IOR 1.33.
    2. b
      Open Transmission › Weight 1. Z › Material Preview: the water goes clear and blue.
    3. c
      Scroll to Settings › tick Raytraced Transmission. Render tab (camera-back icon) › tick Raytracing.

    You should now see: in Material Preview, the drop and the crater rim bend the tiles behind them like glass; the flat pool shows a reflection of the sky instead of the tiles (that is EEVEE; Cycles in Step 16 sees through it).

    What do the four numbers mean?

    Base Color tints the light that passes through (pale blue, like a swimming pool). Roughness 0.02 is a glass-smooth surface. IOR 1.33 is water’s real refractive index: how much it bends light (glass is 1.45, diamond 2.4). Transmission Weight 1 means all the light goes through rather than bouncing off. Raytraced Transmission and Raytracing are the two switches that let EEVEE trace that bent light; without them the water looks like a blue mirror. EEVEE can only trace to things already visible on screen, so the floor hidden under the flat pool stays out of reach and the pool shows the sky; Cycles traces real rays and gets it right, which is why the still is rendered in Cycles.

  2. Tiles, sky and sun

    The Shading workspace, then the World tab and the green light Data tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Floor. Shading tab. Hover the Shader Editor: Shift+A › Texture › Checker Texture. Scale 16, Color1 Hex C9C2B2, Color2 Hex 8F8779. Drag its Color dot to the Principled BSDF’s Base Color dot.
    2. b
      Back in Layout: World tab (red globe) › Color › Hex 9FB4C8, Strength 1.
    3. c
      Outliner › Light. Green bulb tab › Sun, Strength 3. Sidebar › Rotation X 50, Y 10, Z -60.

    You should now see: a tiled floor whose lines wobble where they pass under the water, lit by a pale sky and a sun from the front-left.

    Why tiles?

    Refraction is invisible on a plain floor: bent light looks the same as straight light when everything is one colour. Straight tile lines that kink under the water are the proof the IOR is doing something.

  3. Place the camera

    The Outliner, the sidebar, the green camera Data tab, Numpad 0.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Outliner › Camera. Sidebar Location X 5.2, Y -7, Z 3.7. Rotation X 73, Y 0, Z 35.
    2. b
      Camera tab › Focal Length 42. Numpad 0 to look through it.

    You should now see: the whole pool in frame with the block on the right and room above for the drop and the splash.

    Why those numbers?

    The camera stands about 9 m away, front-right and 3.7 m up, turned 35° to face the pool and tilted down 17°. 42 mm is wide enough to fit the drop at the top of the frame at frame 1 and the crown at frame 22.

End of Part 4. Save.

Part 5

Render

Tools: F12, the render window’s Image menu, the Output tab, Render › Render Animation.

A still of the best frame, and the whole 100-frame splash as a movie.

  1. A still in Cycles, the movie in EEVEE

    The Render tab, the frame box, F12, the render window’s Image menu, the Output tab, the Render menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Render tab › Render Engine: Cycles. Sampling › Render › Max Samples 64, Denoise ticked. Frame 22. Hover the viewport, F12: one to two minutes.
    2. b
      In the render window: Image › Save As › PNG, name it PhysicsLab4_WaterSplash_YourName_render. Esc. Render tab › Render Engine back to EEVEE.
    3. c
      Output tab: Resolution % 50, File Format FFmpeg Video, Container MPEG-4, output folder your Physics labs folder. Render › Render Animation (or Ctrl+F12). About five minutes.
    4. d
      Ctrl+S. Upload the PNG, the .mp4 and the .blend to SEQTA. The cache folder stays on your computer.

    You should now see: a PNG matching Checkpoint D (glass-clear water, tiles bending under it) and a 4-second EEVEE movie of the drop, the crater, the wave and the settle.

    Why two engines?

    Cycles traces real light rays, so it sees the tiles through 30 cm of water and bends them correctly; a frame takes a minute or two. EEVEE is twenty times faster but can only trace to what is already on screen, so the flat pool shows the sky. A still deserves the minute; 100 frames of Cycles would be an hour and a half, so the movie goes to EEVEE. Pick your still frame by scrubbing: 18 to 26 is the crater and rim, 28 to 36 the wave on the walls, 40 to 50 droplets.

End of the lab.

Part 6

Finished early? Pick one

Tools: everything above, used again.

Rule for every experiment: Free All, change one thing, Bake All again. Resolution and the Flows are locked while a bake exists.

Resolution Divisions

The box is 4 m. Slide the number and read the cell size and the bake time.

Open the walls

The wave climbing invisible walls at frame 30 gives the box away. Domain › Fluid › Border Collisions: untick Front, Back, Left and Right. Free All, Bake All. Water that reaches a wall now leaves the domain and vanishes, as if the pool went on forever. Keep Bottom ticked or the pool falls out of the world.

A tap instead of a drop

Drop › Fluid › Flow Behavior: Inflow. A Use Flow tick appears: hover it at frame 40, press I to keyframe it ticked, go to frame 41, untick it, I again. Free All, Bake All: the ball pours water for 40 frames then stops. Open Initial Velocity and set Z -3 to make it a jet.

Spray, foam and bubbles

Domain › Fluid › Particles panel: tick Spray and Foam. Free All, Bake All (slower). Blender adds separate particle systems of fine droplets above the crown and white foam where the water churns. Render: they appear as tiny dots; give the Domain’s new particle systems a white Halo material to see them.

Honey

Domain › Fluid › Diffusion panel: tick it, preset dropdown Honey. Free All, Bake All. The drop lands as a slow blob and the crater never forms. Try Oil and Water to compare; the numbers in the panel are real viscosities.

Slow motion

Domain › Fluid › Settings › Time Scale 0.25: four times slower, so 100 frames show the first second of the splash in detail. Set Timeline End and Cache End to 200 to see more. Free All, Bake All.

Sharper (and slower)

Resolution Divisions 96: 4.2 cm cells, 3.4 times the cells and roughly five times the bake. Start it, then do something else. Compare frame 22 with your 64 version: thinner sheets, more droplets, the same overall shape. The widget above estimates the cost of any number. Below, the other direction: 32 against 64.

Something’s not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

I can’t orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured gizmo itself to orbit. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

There is no Bake All button

Cache › Type is still Replay (or Modular). Set it to All and the button appears. If the panel is greyed out, you are in Edit Mode: Tab out.

Nothing happens when I play

With Replay, the first play is slow and starts from frame 1 only: press Shift+Left first. With All, nothing moves until you Bake All. Also: the mouse must be over the viewport when you press Space.

The box is just a solid grey cube

That is what an unbaked Domain looks like. Alt+Z to see inside; Bake All and the cube is replaced by the water mesh.

The bake finishes instantly and there is no water

No Flow objects, or their Flow Type is still Smoke (the default). Pool and Drop: Physics › Fluid › Type Flow, Flow Type Liquid. Then Free All, Bake All. Also check they are inside the Domain.

The water goes straight through the block

The block is not an Effector (Step 10). Or it is, but it is hollow inside the water: Surface Thickness 0 is fine for a cube; for a thin object tick Is Planar. Free All, Bake All.

Resolution Divisions is greyed out

A bake exists. Cache › Free All, change the number, Bake All.

The bake is taking forever

Resolution too high, or the domain too big, or Spray/Foam on. Esc to stop, Free All, Resolution 48 for a test, 64 for the real thing. The widget in the extensions estimates times.

My bake vanished when I reopened the file

The file was not saved before baking, so the cache went to a temporary folder. Save, Free All, Bake All. Keep the .blend and the cache_fluid folder together; moving one without the other loses the bake.

The water looks like a blue mirror, I can’t see through it

Two switches: Material › Settings › Raytraced Transmission, and Render tab › Raytracing. Both ticked, and Transmission Weight 1 in the material. The drop and the crown should then bend the tiles behind them. The flat pool will still show the sky in EEVEE: that is normal, and Cycles (Step 16) fixes it for the still.

The Cycles render is taking ages

Max Samples left at 4096. Render tab › Sampling › Render › Max Samples 64 with Denoise on; Esc and try again. One frame should take one to three minutes. Never Render Animation in Cycles for this lab.

The water is black or grey in the render

The material went on the wrong object (the Pool or the Drop) instead of the Domain. Click the water mesh, Material tab: it should say Water. Also check Render tab › Raytracing is on.

The grey ball and slab are still in the render

The eye icon only hides them in the viewport. Object tab › Visibility › untick Renders for the Drop and the Pool.

The water looks like it has facets

Right-click the water › Shade Smooth (Step 12). It must be the Domain that is selected.

The water climbs invisible walls

That is the domain: six solid walls by default. It is correct; it is an aquarium. The first extension opens the sides.

The splash is lumpy with no droplets

Resolution 32. Free All, Resolution 64, Bake All. For droplets, 96 or the Spray particles extension.

My render shows a flat pool and a ball

The frame box was on 1. Set it to 22 (or any frame you like) before F12.

The render is dark

Step 14: world colour 9FB4C8 at Strength 1, and the Light set to Sun, Strength 3, Rotation 50, 10, -60.

My render disappeared

A render is only kept if you use Image › Save As in the render window before closing it.

Eight quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You’ll find out straight away whether you’re right.

1Which object type is the only place water can exist?

Right. No domain, no water: it is the box the simulation lives in.

Not quite. Flow makes water and Effector blocks it, but water can only exist inside the Domain.

2Flow Behavior Geometry means

Right. Geometry is a one-off; Inflow keeps pouring.

Not quite. Geometry turns the shape into water once. Inflow is the tap, Outflow the drain.

3Resolution Divisions 64 on a 4 m box gives cells of

Right. 4 m ÷ 64 = 6.25 cm, and nothing smaller than that can show.

Not quite. The number is cells across the longest side: 400 cm ÷ 64 = 6.25 cm.

4Doubling Resolution Divisions makes the bake roughly

Right. Eight times the cells, and each needs about twice the time steps.

Not quite. Cells go up by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, and the smaller cells need about twice as many time steps: around 16.

5Why was the pool slab made wider than the box?

Right. Only the part inside the Domain counts.

Not quite. Anything outside the Domain is simply ignored, so an oversized slab guarantees the pool fills the box edge to edge.

6The Floor object has no Fluid physics. What does the water do at the floor?

Right. The water never sees the Floor; it sees the Domain’s wall.

Not quite. Objects without Fluid physics are invisible to the water. The Domain’s own bottom border is the floor.

7Cache Type All with Bake All

Right. That folder is why you saved first.

Not quite. Replay is the one that keeps nothing. All bakes everything to the cache folder beside your file.

8Which two switches make EEVEE show bent light through the water?

Right. One is per material, the other is for the whole render.

Not quite. IOR says how much to bend; Raytraced Transmission and Raytracing let EEVEE actually trace it.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

A real drop of water this size would break into spray and foam long before it hit. What in the simulation stops that happening, and which extension gets closest to fixing it?

Upload to SEQTA — Physics Lab 4

Upload PhysicsLab4_WaterSplash_YourName.blend, PhysicsLab4_WaterSplash_YourName_render.png and the .mp4. The .blend should contain the Domain (Liquid, 64 divisions, cache All, baked), the Pool and Drop as Liquid Flows, the Block as an Effector, the water material with Raytraced Transmission, the tiled floor, the world colour, the sun and the camera.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

Two lessons. Lesson 1: Parts 1–3 (Quick Liquid, the set, physics, bake). Start the bake before the end of the lesson if possible; at Resolution 64 it takes two to five minutes on a school laptop. Lesson 2: Parts 4–5 (material, lighting, camera, render) and extensions. The Cycles still takes one to two minutes at 64 samples; the 50% EEVEE movie about five minutes.

How the pictures were made

Every step was built exactly as written in Blender 5.2.2 and the fluid settings were verified against the Blender source (panel names, defaults, enum labels). The liquid itself was simulated with Mantaflow 0.13, the standalone build of the solver that Blender embeds, with the lab’s settings mirrored (4 m domain, 64 divisions, FLIP 0.97, CFL 2, time steps 1–4, narrow band 3, particle radius 1, 8–16 particles per cell, mesh at 2× resolution with the Final generator). Blender’s own bake could not be run in the headless build used to make this page, so a student’s bake will match in behaviour and timing but not vertex for vertex. The water meshes were then loaded into the lab scene and rendered in Blender 5.2.2 (Workbench for the viewport look, EEVEE for the filmstrip, Cycles for the still), with the lab’s material, lights and camera.

What changed from the original sheet

  • It is a splash now. The original used a single cube with Inflow inside an empty domain, which pours water continuously and slowly fills the box: no drop, no crater, no wave. The rebuilt scene is a drop (Geometry flow) into a standing pool (a second Geometry flow), the classic splash.
  • The Effector was missing. The learning objectives promised Flow and Effector objects but no step created an effector. The Block is the effector, and the wave hitting it is visible in every checkpoint.
  • Exact numbers replace “scale and move the domain to enclose the cube”. Every object has a typed location and scale; the drop height and impact frame are calculated for students; the domain size is explained in terms of cell size.
  • Save first, and why. The fluid cache is a folder beside the .blend; the original saved at the end (Step 10), after baking, which puts the cache in a temporary folder that is lost.
  • The material is fixed for Blender 4.x/5.x. “Transmission 0.95” is now the Transmission Weight input; Raytraced Transmission (material Settings) and Raytracing (Render tab) are added, without which EEVEE shows an opaque blue mirror. The material goes on the Domain, which is the fluid mesh (the original said “select the fluid mesh”).
  • Hiding sources is done with both the Outliner eye and Visibility › Renders; the original used the eye only, so the flow cube would still appear in renders. Shade Smooth on the domain is added (the mesh is flat-shaded otherwise).
  • Replay vs Modular vs All is explained with a card; the original mentioned “Type to All” without saying what the alternatives do, and “Use Flow” and “Flow Source Mesh”, which are defaults, are dropped from the steps (Use Flow is only shown for Inflow/Outflow in Blender 5).
  • Camera, lighting and animation output are added; the original rendered with the default camera and light and had no movie. The still is rendered in Cycles (64 samples, denoised, one to two minutes) because EEVEE’s screen-space refraction cannot see the floor under the flat pool; the movie stays in EEVEE for speed. Both looks are shown in the checkpoints so students know what to expect from each.

Where students usually get stuck

Flow Type left on Smoke (the bake finishes instantly with no water). Cache Type left on Replay (no Bake All button). Changing resolution with a bake present (greyed out). Pressing Space over the Properties editor. Putting the water material on the Pool instead of the Domain. Forgetting Raytracing in the Render tab. Baking in an unsaved file.

Quiz answers

1 Domain. 2 Becomes water once. 3 6.25 cm. 4 About 16 times. 5 Water outside the box is ignored. 6 The Domain’s bottom wall. 7 Saves everything beside the .blend. 8 Raytraced Transmission and Raytracing.
